**Key Takeaways**


- Pay transparency is the practice of openly sharing how pay is set and what roles pay, with candidates, employees, or both. It runs from posting a range in a job ad to publishing every employee's pay.
- The level you choose matters less than whether your compensation data can support it. Each rung requires something specific: a range for every role, a documented rationale for every range, and managers who can explain both.
- Regulation is setting the floor. As of 2026, 17 U.S. states and Washington, D.C. have pay transparency laws in effect, and the EU directive adds pay gap reporting from 2027.
- The payoff is real when the data is ready. Transparency exposes inconsistencies, so the companies that benefit are the ones that fixed their bands before they published them.


Pay transparency is the practice of openly sharing information about how compensation is determined and what jobs pay. At its narrowest, it means including a salary range in a job posting. At its widest, it means every employee can see what every other employee earns and how that number was set.


Most organizations sit somewhere in between. Where you sit is a strategic decision with compliance, culture, and data implications.


This guide covers what pay transparency means in practice, the five levels companies operate at, and what a pay transparency policy needs to contain. It also covers the part most explainers skip: what your compensation data has to be able to do before each level is safe to adopt.


## What is pay transparency?


Pay transparency is the degree to which an organization discloses pay information. Three things can be disclosed, and the combinations define the level.


- **Pay ranges.** The minimum, midpoint, and maximum for a role or level, shared with candidates, with the employee in the role, or with everyone.
- **Pay-setting criteria.** How a range was built (market benchmark, level, location) and how an individual moves within it (performance, tenure, promotion).
- **Individual pay.** What specific people earn, from an employee's own number up to a fully open payroll.


You will also see the practice called wage transparency, salary transparency, or compensation transparency. The terms are interchangeable. Regulators tend to say "pay" or "wage", and total rewards teams say "compensation" when equity and bonus are in scope.


One thing pay transparency is not: a single policy that a company either has or lacks. A company posting ranges in job ads because state law requires it is transparent.


So is a company publishing its full pay bands internally. The second has done roughly ten times the work.


## The five levels of pay transparency


Most organizations climb this ladder one rung at a time. Each rung has a data requirement the previous one did not.


Level What candidates and employees see What your compensation data has to support


**1. Pay secrecy** Nothing. Employees know their own pay; ranges exist, if at all, in HR's spreadsheet. Nothing yet, which is why this level feels safe and why it hides every inconsistency.


**2. Ranges on request** Candidates get a range if they ask, or after the first interview. Employees can ask for their own range. A defined range for every open role, current enough that the number given out matches the offer that follows.


**3. Ranges in postings** Every job ad carries a pay range. This is the legal floor in most U.S. transparency states. A range for every role, including the ones nobody is hiring for, because employees compare their pay with the posted range for their own job. Ranges tight enough to be credible. A $90,000 to $200,000 posting signals that no range exists.


**4. Bands shared internally** Employees can see the full range structure: every level, the midpoints, and the criteria for moving between them. Every employee mapped to a level, every range anchored to a market benchmark with a written rationale, and a plan for anyone sitting below their range minimum, because they will find out.


**5. Open pay** Individual pay is visible, either internally or publicly, with the formula that produced it. A formula-driven pay structure where the same inputs always give the same output, and a comfort with the questions that follow. Rare outside a small set of companies that built pay this way from the start.


The ladder is cumulative. A company cannot publish bands internally (level 4) without a range for every role (level 3). It cannot post credible ranges if those ranges were never built against the market (level 2).


Most of the difficulty companies report with transparency is really the difficulty of a level they skipped.


## Choosing a level


Four factors decide where an organization should sit, and they pull in different directions.


**Compliance sets the floor.** If you hire in a state or country with a posting law, level 3 is not optional for those roles. As of 2026, 17 U.S. states and Washington, D.C. have[pay transparency laws by state](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/pay-transparency-the-ultimate-guide) in effect, most requiring ranges in job postings ([GovDocs](https://www.govdocs.com/pay-transparency-laws/) ). The[EU pay transparency directive](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/eu-pay-transparency-directive) adds range disclosure before interview and gender pay gap reporting from 2027.


**Readiness sets the ceiling.** Moving above the level your data supports is where transparency goes wrong. Publishing bands exposes every employee below their minimum and every pair of peers paid inconsistently, all at once.


Fix the structure first. Many companies find the fixing was the valuable part.


**Culture decides the pace.** Organizations that already talk openly about how decisions are made absorb transparency easily. Where pay has always been a private negotiation, managers need training before anything is published.


WTW research cited in Pave's work on[compensation communication](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/from-offer-to-vesting-compensation-value) found that 84% of employers rely on managers to communicate pay, and only 38% believe they have trained them well. That gap is what turns a transparency rollout into a trust problem.


**Talent strategy decides the direction.** Posting ranges filters candidates before they apply, and the SHRM figures in the next section show the upside.


The trade? A range that looks low for the market filters out the people you most wanted to talk to. That is an argument for benchmarking the range properly before posting it.


## Benefits of pay transparency


In today's workplace, pay transparency serves multiple strategic purposes beyond legal compliance. Organizations that embrace transparency often report increased trust between employees and management, reduced negotiation friction during hiring, and greater ability to attract candidates who align with their compensation philosophy. According to SHRM research, 70% of companies that[list pay ranges on their job postings](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/all-things-work/pay-transparency-equity) found that it led to more applications, and 66% said the quality of applicants increased. Transparency can also help companies identify and address pay inequities more effectively by making disparities more visible.


Pay transparency also plays a crucial role in empowering employees to make informed career decisions. When workers understand how compensation is determined and what opportunities exist for advancement, they can better advocate for themselves and make strategic choices about their career paths. This clarity can lead to improved job satisfaction and reduced turnover as employees feel more confident they're being compensated fairly.


> Companies that proactively embrace transparency rather than waiting for legislative requirements often find themselves better positioned to attract and retain talent, build trust with employees, and create more equitable workplaces.


## Challenges to implementing pay transparency


However, implementing pay transparency presents significant challenges. Organizations must carefully balance transparency with privacy concerns and competitive considerations. Many companies also struggle to explain legitimate pay differences that result from factors like experience, performance, or location. Finally, there is the challenge of managing employee reactions to learning about pay differences, which can sometimes lead to decreased motivation, increased conflict, or legal action.


Technical implementation poses another hurdle. Companies need robust systems to track and communicate compensation data accurately. They must develop clear[compensation philosophies](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/compensation-philosophy-what-it-is-and-how-to-build-one) and frameworks that can withstand scrutiny. Additionally, managers need training to have productive conversations about pay and handle challenging questions from their teams.


Cultural change may be the most significant hurdle. Moving from a culture of pay secrecy to transparency requires significant change management. Organizations must build trust with employees, prepare for[difficult conversations](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/compensation-conversations-are-a-big-opportunity-to-drive-trust-heres-how-hr-teams-can-prepare) , and develop communication strategies that explain their compensation practices effectively. This often requires a fundamental shift in how organizations think about and discuss money.


## Pay transparency and pay equity


Transparency and equity are different things that reinforce each other. Transparency is disclosure.


[Pay equity](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/what-is-pay-equity-and-why-does-it-matter) is the absence of unjustified pay differences. Disclosure makes differences visible, which is what forces the equity work.


The differences are larger than most leadership teams expect. Pave's[gender pay gap data](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/equal-pay-day-2025-gender-pay-gap-insights) shows an unadjusted gap in base salary of 22%.


It narrows to 4% once job family, level, and location are controlled for. The role-adjusted gap in equity is 16%.


A company at level 4 will have those numbers surfaced by its own employees within weeks of publishing bands. A company at level 1 has the same gaps and no visibility of them. The second position is only quieter.


## What a pay transparency policy contains


A pay transparency policy is the document that says which level the company operates at, what is disclosed to whom, and how pay decisions are explained. A usable one has five parts.


1. **Scope.** Which information is shared (ranges, criteria, individual pay), with which audiences (candidates, employees, managers, the public), and in which jurisdictions, since the legal floor differs by location.
2. **The pay structure it refers to.** The levels, the ranges, and where they come from. A policy that promises "market-based ranges" has to be able to name the market data behind them and how often it is refreshed.
3. **Pay-setting criteria.** How someone is placed within a range at hire, and how they move: performance, tenure, promotion, market adjustment. This is the section employees read most closely and the one regulators increasingly require.
4. **Manager guidance.** What managers can and cannot say about pay, with the answers to the questions that will come ("why is the new hire paid more than me?") written down in advance.
5. **The review cycle.** When ranges are re-benchmarked, when the policy is revisited, and who owns it.


The policy should be shorter than the work behind it. If writing section two is difficult, that is the diagnostic: the ranges are not ready to be published yet.


## Preparing the data before the disclosure


Whatever level you are targeting, the sequence that works is the same.


1. **Map every role to a level.** Any level above the first needs a[job architecture](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/what-is-job-architecture) , so that "the range for this job" is a defined thing.
2. **Build or re-benchmark the ranges.** Anchor every[salary range](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/what-is-a-salary-range-guide) to a current market median for the level and location, with a documented target position (for example, midpoint at the 50th percentile). A range built on a survey from two years ago will not survive the first employee who checks it against a competitor's posting.
3. **Find and cost the outliers.** Everyone below their range minimum, and every peer group with unexplained spread. Fix them before publishing, or publish with a dated plan to fix them. Publishing without either is how transparency creates the trust problem it was meant to solve.
4. **Train the managers.** Every manager should be able to explain the range, the criteria, and the employee's position within it, in that order.
5. **Disclose, then hold the line.** Once ranges are public, every offer and every raise is measured against them. The structure has to be maintained, which is the case for running ranges out of a system instead of a spreadsheet.

### Frequently asked questions (FAQs):


##### What does pay transparency mean?


Pay transparency means an organization openly shares information about how pay is set and what roles pay.


In practice it ranges from posting a salary range in a job ad, which is now required in many U.S. states, to sharing the full range structure with employees, to making individual pay visible. The term covers the whole spectrum; the level a company operates at is a choice.


##### Is pay transparency good or bad?


It depends on the state of the pay structure being made transparent. Where ranges are benchmarked and consistently applied, transparency builds trust, speeds up hiring, and surfaces small inequities before they become structural.


Where ranges are missing or inconsistent, transparency exposes that immediately, which is why the preparation matters more than the disclosure. The direction of regulation makes the question less optional every year.


##### What should a pay transparency policy include?


Five things: the scope of what is disclosed and to whom; the pay structure the policy refers to, including where the ranges come from; the criteria for setting and moving pay within a range; guidance for managers on how to discuss pay; and the cycle for re-benchmarking ranges and reviewing the policy. The policy is only as strong as the ranges behind it.


##### Is wage transparency the same as pay transparency?


Yes. Wage transparency, salary transparency, and compensation transparency all refer to the same practice of disclosing pay information. Regulators and hourly-workforce contexts tend to say "wage", salaried contexts say "salary", and total rewards teams say "compensation" when the disclosure covers bonus and equity as well as base pay.
